source.title: Learning from i.i.d. data under model miss-specification

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the paper’s main sections, appendices, and tables; no truncation or garbling prevents reading the reported results.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports test-set predictive performance for Bayesian-like variational and ensemble methods under model misspecification, a different setting and mechanism from the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports test log-likelihoods for Fashion-MNIST and CIFAR-10, but does not test random-label memorization, width beyond interpolation, convolutional versus fully connected architectures, optimizer comparisons, batch-size effects, dropout, sharpness measures, or removal of memorized examples. The measured outcome is test predictive log-likelihood, not a training-test error gap.
record.test_reason: The study analyzes Bayesian model averaging under model misspecification and compares predictive log-likelihoods of its proposed methods. Neither its experiments nor its theoretical arguments test or rely on any of V1–V8. Using Adam, mini-batches and an MLP does not test optimizer, batch-size or architecture comparisons.
record.authors_conclusion: The record broadly captures the authors' empirical conclusion: second-order objectives generally improve predictive performance, tighter objectives generally improve it further, and ensembles perform best overall in the real-data experiments. The authors identify CIFAR-10 classification as a setting where all variational methods underperform MAP. Their central theoretical conclusion is that Bayesian posterior concentration can be suboptimal for predictive model averaging under misspecification. Table D.1 additionally shows that PAC2 slightly underperforms standard variational inference on Fashion-MNIST classification and PAC2T underperforms PAC2 on CIFAR-10 classification, qualifying the empirical ordering stated in the prose.
record.recipe_differences: Studies Bayesian model averaging and newly proposed PAC2 variational and ensemble methods under model misspecification; uses test predictive log-likelihood rather than train-test error gaps. Real-data models are MLPs with 20 hidden units trained using Adam.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary by dataset, prediction task, and method; for CIFAR-10 supervised classification the authors state variational approaches do not outperform MAP.

fits_no_version.finding: In both datasets' self-supervised tasks, PAC2 improves test predictive log-likelihood over standard variational inference, and PAC2T improves further. In Fashion-MNIST classification, PAC2 is slightly worse than standard variational inference (-3610.37 versus -3598.26), while PAC2T is better (-3558.94). In CIFAR-10 classification, both proposed methods improve over standard variational inference but remain worse than MAP; PAC2T also performs worse than PAC2.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Second-order PAC-Bayes variational objectives can improve predictive log-likelihood over standard variational inference under model misspecification, with gains depending on task, dataset and objective.

record.problems: The empirical evaluation uses MLPs with 20 hidden units and reports aggregate test log-likelihood without uncertainty estimates. It does not report training error alongside test error for the listed claim versions. The CIFAR-10 supervised classification variational results do not improve over MAP, which the authors attribute tentatively to prior specification or a simplistic variational family.
record.rows_left_out: Table D.2 reports ensemble results across datasets, tasks, and ensemble sizes. Those results were omitted to keep the extraction focused on the variational comparisons in Table D.1; the paper states ensemble methods outperform the rest overall and provides detailed Table D.2 values.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting, natural-label held-out accuracy, and chance-level held-out accuracy with random labels.
Width sweeps and test error beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks and the contribution of local connectivity or initialization.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizers under different tuning, weight-decay or switching recipes.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Effects of dropout, training-set size, augmentation and removal of weight decay.
Magnitude-aware weight-perturbation sharpness, its correlation with generalization gaps, and comparison with other measures.
Removal of memorized training examples versus random removal and subsequent test accuracy.

record.verdict_notes: All 24 numerical values match Table D.1. They are method-performance results rather than evidence for any supplied claim version. Predictive log-likelihood can measure generalization, but these experiments lack the specific comparisons V1–V8 require. The predictive-disagreement variance term is not V7's magnitude-aware weight sharpness. Ensemble size is not V2's network width. Table D.2 is already declared in rows_left_out, and no omitted result bears on V1–V8.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparisons.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets.
Removal of memorized examples and retraining.
